worksheet.title: Match the Algorithm
worksheet.subtitle: Read the steps and name the job
worksheet.learning_goal: I can match an algorithm to the job its steps do.

parts.title: An algorithm does a job
parts.text: Every algorithm does a job. Read the steps and figure out the job. Match each algorithm to its job. One job has no algorithm — you will write it.

parts.title: What job is Algorithm 1?
parts.prompt: Read the steps. Which job does Algorithm 1 do? Write the job.

parts.title: What job is Algorithm 2?
parts.prompt: Which job does Algorithm 2 do? Write the job.

parts.title: You try — write the leftover one
parts.prompt: The leftover job is 'get a drink'. Write an algorithm for it — 3 or 4 steps in order, one per line.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: The steps of an algorithm tell you what job it does. Reading code to figure out what it does is a big part of being a coder.

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students read two sets of steps, work out which job each one does, then write the steps for a leftover job. Reading a plan to figure out what it accomplishes is a key thinking skill. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer — paper and a pencil. You read each prompt aloud. Optional: cut the steps into cards so students can physically slide them into order before writing.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Read a set of steps and ask: "what job is this?"
2. Do one together. Algorithm 1 is washing hands; Algorithm 2 is feeding the dog.
3. Let them try. Students write the steps for the leftover job (getting a drink).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — Algorithm 1 = wash hands (wet, soap, rinse, dry). Exercise 2 — Algorithm 2 = feed the dog (get the bowl, scoop the food, put it down, call the dog).
Exercise 3 — get a drink: a sample is get a cup, turn on the tap, fill the cup, turn off the tap. Accept any 3–4 sensible ordered steps.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: guessing the job from one step. Read all the steps before deciding.
Make it easier: give two job names to choose between.
Make it harder: ask them to add a step that would make the job clearer.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
In plain terms: students put step-by-step instructions in the right order to get a result.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read a set of steps, change or reorder one, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child names the job for each set of steps and writes a sensible ordered plan for the leftover one.
